summary:
See things move in the sky. SkyShift fetches small cutouts of any sky position from NASA's SPHEREx mission (via the public IRSA archive), aligns them, and lets you blink between visits to spot nearby stars and brown dwarfs drifting against the background.

An optional overlay circles stars already known to ESA's Gaia catalogue (Data Release 3), moved to where Gaia's measured motion predicts they are on each image's date, so anything moving without a circle stands out.
details:
SkyShift lets anyone watch the sky change. Pick a patch of sky, and SkyShift fetches every image NASA's SPHEREx mission has taken of it, lines them up, and

plays them as a short film. Things that move or change brightness, such as nearby stars, brown dwarfs, asteroids and comets, stand out against the fixed background.

How it works:

- Finds every SPHEREx exposure of the position in the NASA/IPAC Infrared ScienceArchive, aligns the cutouts north-up and combines them per visit.

- Plays the visits as a video, or subtracts one from another so anything thatmoved shows as an orange and blue pair.

- Click any object to plot its spectrum from 0.75 to 5 microns across all six detectors, downloadable as CSV.

- The same click answers "is this already known?" by checking SIMBAD, ESA's Gaia catalogue and the SkyBoT list of asteroids and comets.

Benefits and impact:

- SPHEREx re-images the whole sky repeatedly, far more than professionals can inspect by eye.

- Anyone can explore it in a browser, with no software to install and no astronomy background.

- A built-in tutorial teaches what to look for, and "next patch" and "random patch" buttons mean nobody needs to know a coordinate.

- The aim is to let the public help search for overlooked moving objects.

Tools: Python (FastAPI, Astropy, reproject, NumPy, SciPy), plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, hosted on Vercel. Claude Code (AI) assisted with coding.

Creativity: Instead of showing a catalogue, SkyShift shows the motion itself, then lets one click turn curiosity into a measurement and a verdict.

What we considered:

- Honesty about limits: the app says when a catalogue did not answer, flags doubtful measurements, and explains when an object is too bright for the detector.

- Beginners, phone layouts, archive rate limits, and shareable links so a find can be shown to others.
dataRefs: SPHEREx data at NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA)
IRSA image search API (Simple Image Access)
